title: A Single Architecture for Representing Invariance Under Any Space Group
claim: Symmetry constraints on a Fourier lattice become graph edges, and each connected component yields one invariant basis function.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, gray backgrounds, headline text above each panel
description: Three gray panels read left to right, each with a bold-keyword heading. Panel 1 shows a 2D grid of black dots on axes: the lattice of nonzero Fourier coefficients induced by translation invariance. Panel 2 shows a wallpaper-group pattern 'pg' of F glyphs, some mirrored, in a diamond tiling. Next to it, the same lattice has red and blue arcs joining points, which are weighted edges for the constraints from other isometries. Panel 3 shows a connected component as a small red or blue arc between two points. Beside each is a heatmap of the resulting basis function (vertical stripes, and a checkerboard-like blob grid). Colored formulas e1(x) and e2(x) label the basis functions in blue and red. The eye goes first to the colorful heatmaps and arcs.
caption: We construct the Fourier basis for $G$-invariant functions using a dual representation in terms of graphs. The translations in a crystallographic group $G$ give rise to a discrete lattice of points corresponding to the Fourier series. We represent constraints induced by additional isometries as weighted edges between these points. For wallpaper group pg, which contains the translations and glide reflections present in the tiling pattern, we get edges of weight $-1$ (red) and $+1$ (blue). Each clique in the resulting graph can be expanded as one of the pictured Fourier basis functions.
abstract: Incorporating known symmetries in data into machine learning models has consistently improved predictive accuracy, robustness, and generalization. However, achieving exact invariance to specific symmetries typically requires designing bespoke architectures for each group, limiting scalability and preventing knowledge transfer across related symmetries. In the case of the space groups, symmetries critical to modeling crystalline solids in materials science and condensed matter physics, this challenge is particularly salient as there are 230 such groups in three dimensions. In this work we present a new approach to such crystallographic symmetries by developing a single machine learning architecture that is capable of adapting its weights automatically to enforce invariance to any input space group. Our approach is based on constructing symmetry-adapted Fourier bases through an explicit characterization of constraints that group operations impose on Fourier coefficients. Encoding these constraints into a neural network layer enables weight sharing across different space groups, allowing the model to leverage structural similarities between groups and overcome data sparsity when limited measurements are available for specific groups. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in achieving competitive performance on material property prediction tasks and performing zero-shot learning to generalize to unseen groups.
